newsitem.title: USA: PRESS DIGEST - Wall Street Journal - Feb 10.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - Wall Street Journal - Feb 10.

text.p: The following stories were reported in Monday's electronic version of The Wall Street Journal:
* The G-7 nations expressed unity in their desire to halt the rapid rise of the dollar after U.S. Treasury Secretery Robert Rubin indicated that the dollar had risen high enough.
* A White House aviation panel is recommending billions of dollars in spending to increase airport security and accelerate improvements in the air-traffic control system.
* Payrolls rose by 271,000 workers in January, compared to 261,000 added in December, yet there were few signs of inflation.
* USAir is asking pilots who would stay with its main operation to take a 12.5 percent cut in pay.
* The Federal Communications Commission rejected a key part of Ameritech's request to offer long-distance services, almost ensuring that the Bell will have to withdraw its landmark application.

* The tobacco industry faces an unprecedented array of courtroom fights, beginning Monday in Greensboro, North Carolina, where the firms will challenge federal rules to constrain how cigarettes are sold.
* A former Kodak employee denied he would sell company secrets in a tape the company secretly made as part of its racketeering case against him.
* Western Resources' $2 billion pact to buy Kansas City Power & Light calls for KCPL's chairman to join Western as a vice chairman.
* The Dow Jones industrials rose 82.74 to 6,855.80 Friday. Bonds also advanced, and the dollar was mixed.
* Microsoft said it would no longer create new versions of its Windows NT operating system on the Power PC chip family.
* A jury ordered Harley-Davidson to pay $9.9 million to a man who said a stuck cruise control on his motorcycle caused an accident.
* Oracle will announce a $500 gadget that will let its customers check users' fingerprints before letting them log on to their computer.
* Canadian 88 withdrew its hostile bid for Morrison Petroleums just days before a regulatory hearing on whether Canadian 88 broke securities rules before the offer.
* Enron says it is pursuing several new projects in India despite its five-year struggle to win approval for a power plant there.
* If there is to be a me-too transaction modeled on a merger of Morgan Stanley and Dean, Witter Discover, one of the likeliest candidates may be PaineWebber.

After Dean Witter, PaineWebber is the next largest independent U.S. brokerage focused heavily on individual investors. It would be a logical partner for any securities firm, such as Goldman Sachs, Salomon Bros or Lehman Bros, specializing in institutional clients. -- Heard on the Street.

* Suddenly, the road to success in the emerging markets is looking bumpier. Bonds from developing countries known as emerging markets turned heads during the past two years. Last year's 39 percent gain and 1995's 27 percent return give emerging-markets bonds the unique distinction of outperforming even the stock market's impressive returns.

This year began with a bang, with J.P. Morgan's emerging-markets index scoring a return of 28 percent in January. But in just the past few weeks problems have emerged, and although more money is chasing the emerging-market sector the best gains may already have been achieved, many analysts say. -- Credit Markets.
-- New York newsdesk 212-859-1610.
